notes.meaning: The psalm opens with a joyful shout: the Lord is King! He is pictured like a king putting on royal robes, and like a soldier tying on a belt and armour, ready to act. His power is His own. He did not borrow it from anyone. Because He rules, the world stands firm and cannot be shaken loose from His care.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe this psalm also looks ahead to a future thousand-year reign of the Messiah on earth, called the Millennium.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine read God's 'girding' as a picture of Christ tying on a towel to wash His disciples' feet. On this reading, God's strength is shown in humility. He read the world that 'cannot be moved' as the faithful spread across the whole earth.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Orthodox churches sing this verse ('The Lord is King: He is robed in majesty') before the readings at Saturday evening prayer. Their Bibles number this psalm 92.

notes.meaning: God's throne is no new thing. It was set up long ago, before anything else existed. God Himself has no beginning and will have no end. He made the world, so He has every right to rule it. No rebel can overturn a King like that.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine applied 'You are from everlasting' to Christ. Though He was born in time, He is eternal.

notes.meaning: The writer pictures roaring floods and pounding waves. Most older writers see these as a picture of nations and wicked people raging against God and His people, wave after wave. The writer does not talk back to the waves. He tells the Lord about them. Some also apply the picture to the storms of fear and strong feelings inside our own hearts.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: In the ancient world, floodwaters often stood for chaos. Canaanite stories told of the god Baal beating the sea god. Early readers may have heard this psalm as saying the Lord alone rules the waters.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine read the 'rivers' as the apostles. Filled with the Spirit, they lifted up their voices to preach. He read the raging sea as the persecution that followed.

notes.meaning: However loud the waves roar, the Lord is mightier still. 'On high' means He rules over them and they cannot reach Him. The threats of God's enemies are mostly noise, more sound than real power. That is real comfort for God's people in every storm.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine saw the boat as the Church and the sea as the world. Christ walks over the waves, and rulers and kings came to believe in Him.

notes.meaning: God's 'testimonies' are His word to us, both His promises and His commands. They are completely sure. You could say they are 'very Amen-ed.' Holiness, meaning being set apart for God and pure, is the fitting beauty of His house. That house is His temple, His church and His people, and this holds true for all time.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Orthodox churches sing 'Holiness befits Thy house, O Lord, forevermore!' as one of the verses at Saturday evening prayer.
